newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US official calls for budget cuts at ILO, WHO.
newsitem.headline: US official calls for budget cuts at ILO, WHO.

text.p: A senior U.S. official called on Tuesday for budget cuts of five to 10 percent at the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and World Health Organisation (WHO).

Princeton Lyman, Assistant Secretary of State for International organisation affairs, said the cuts would not have a "detrimental impact" on the vital programmes of the two Geneva-based specialised U.N. agencies.
In line with its aim of reducing the U.S. contribution to the U.N. regular budget, Washington was also seeking to cut its share of the ILO and WHO budgets to 20 from 25 percent, he said.
Lyman told Reuters before flying to Rome, home of the U.N. food agency: "I am on my way to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) to say the same thing".
Addressing a news conference in Geneva, he said:

"We think that both the WHO and the ILO have room for considerable improvement both in prioritising their programmes and finding more efficient ways to carry out their programmes that would result not only in better impact but we think room for reducing those budgets."
Lyman added: "We estimate that between five and 10 percent reductions are possible in these specialised agencies without having a detrimental impact on their programmes."
The 191 member states of the WHO will discuss the 1998-99 budget at the annual world health assembly being held in Geneva from May 5-14. No spokesman was available to provide figures.
For years, Western countries have criticised the management of WHO's Japanese director-general Hiroshi Nakajima.

Lyman said: "Quite frankly an awful lot can be done just in changing the way the WHO does business -- the structure of it, the division of it into so many different departments, the relationship between the centre and the regions," he said.

On ILO and WHO, he said: "Obviously it is not popular to ask anybody to reduce budgets. It is particularly difficult if there is a perception -- and I have to be candid there is a perception that all we want to do is reduce budgets and in effect reduce development programmes and impact in the economic and social areas. That isn't the case."
